newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian analysts divided on credit rating level.
newsitem.headline: Estonian analysts divided on credit rating level.

text.p: Despite Estonia's reputation as the economic powerhouse of the Baltics, some analysts were unsure whether it will get an investment grade credit rating due to worries on public sector and current account deficits.
The central bank on Wednesday announced that it has finally decided to ask for a credit rating after several months of speculation and delay.

Commercial banks expect the rating to be higher or at least equal to the investment grade BBB given by Standard and Poor's to neighbour Latvia although some analysts said that Estonia's macroeconomic indicators were not as good.

"Estonia's foreign debt burden is small but the situation in the current account deficit and the balance of payments is not as good as in Latvia," Ardo Hansson, economist and adviser to the prime minister, told Reuters.
Estonia's current account deficit reached 5.3 billion kroons in 1996 compared to 2.1 billion a year ago.
Hansson also warned that a rating would make it easier for Estonian banks to take more foreign loans.
"It is bad in the present context, because banks are borrowing too much already," Hansson said.
Hansson has several times warned of overheating in the small Estonian economy as banks lending rates rise rapidly.
"If the rating is worse, it will have a sobering effect because Western financiers will be less interested," he added.
Tallinna Pank financial markets head Martti Siimann said a good economic background will help Estonia to a better rating.
"I think it will be at least equal to or a bit higher than Latvia and Lithuania," he said.
"Estonia is not so good in terms of macroeconomic indicators but the general economic background and climate will enable the country to get a better rating," he added.
Estonia's gross domestic product posted a four percent rise in 1996 after a 4.3 percent rise in 1995.
Inflation is falling, and was down to a year-on-year 9.1 percent in March compared with 28.3 percent in March 1995.

Margus Schults, vice-president of Uhispank, said that if bank rating agency Thomson Bankwatch gave Estonia the highest credit rating of ex-Soviet Union countries, then a rating from Moody's or from S&P should be higher as well.
Thomson gave Estonia a sovereign BBB- rating in April.
Commercial banks said they saw only a positive impact if the rating is good and Schults said it should encourage investment.
"It will broaden the range of investors, because investors active here are already positive that the country is worth investing into," he said.
Erkki Raasuke, interest rate products manager and financial risks head with leading bank Hansapank said interest towards assets in kroons should rise with a good rating.
"The closest benchmark is Latvia with BBB...if we get better, then it's good news, if at a lower level, then its bad news," he said.
